analysis.one_liner: Requires private equity firms to win government approval before buying health care companies and disclose their finances.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to license and police private equity in hospitals, nursing homes, and doctor practices went to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private equity funds to get a license from the Department of Health and Human Services before buying or investing in hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, or doctor practices. It would have forced for-profit health care owners to report their debts, fees, dividends, staffing levels, wage cuts, closures, and political spending to the government, with the data made public. It would also have blocked health care sale-leaseback deals with real estate investment trusts that weaken a hospital's finances, required hospitals to give 90 days' notice before closing or dropping services, and told bankruptcy courts to put preserving local care ahead of other goals.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities where hospitals, nursing homes, or doctor practices have been bought by private equity or are at risk of closing; health workers whose wages, benefits, and pensions would be better protected; and taxpayers, who would see the finances of firms living off Medicare and Medicaid dollars made public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and communities near at-risk hospitals

how_it_helps.text: Private equity funds would need an HHS license to buy or invest in a health care entity, and the Secretary could deny or revoke a license for price gauging, understaffing, or creating access barriers, with revoked firms forced to divest.

For-profit health care owners would have to report debts, debt-to-equity ratios, fees charged by private equity funds, dividends extracted, staffing ratios, wage and benefit cuts, closures, and all political spending, and the Secretary would make the data public.
Private equity-controlled firms could be required to set up escrow accounts with at least five years of funding to pay staff and support nearby providers if a facility closes or services are cut.

Hospitals would have to notify HHS at least 90 days before closing or discontinuing services, could not drop essential services during that window, and would have to file a public mitigation plan subject to a 45-day comment period.

Hospitals could no longer sell or lease their buildings to a real estate investment trust on terms that would weaken the hospital's long-term finances, and rent from health care properties would no longer count toward REIT tax status.

In bankruptcy, workers' pension withdrawal liability would be paid first, and bankruptcy courts would have to give substantial weight to whether a plan preserves regional access to care and keeps providers and staff.
Registered investment companies would be barred from stripping assets from health care entities or undermining care quality and access.
License application fees and penalties would fund the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving low-income patients.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, health care real estate investment trusts, and for-profit hospital, nursing home, and physician-practice owners would bear licensing, escrow, reporting, and penalty costs and could see deals blocked. Supporters of a lighter touch argue some capital could also retreat from struggling rural facilities if the approval process makes deals too risky.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity, health care REITs, and for-profit operators

drawbacks.text: The main enforcement penalty for most violations is capped at $10,000 per violation, which is small for large firms, so much of the bill's teeth depends on licensing and revocation rather than fines.

An approval process and mandatory escrow accounts could discourage investment in financially struggling hospitals and nursing homes, the facilities that critics of the bill would say most need outside capital.

Key terms, including which services count as essential and what counts as price gauging or understaffing, are left to determination by the Secretary, giving wide discretion to whichever administration is in power.
The extensive reporting requirements apply to all for-profit health care owners, not only private equity, creating a compliance burden for smaller operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a broad attempt to police how private equity and for-profit owners run health care facilities, relying mostly on transparency and a licensing gate rather than price controls. Its main benefits would flow to patients and workers at facilities most exposed to buyouts and closures, and its costs would fall on investors and for-profit operators. The honest objections are that the penalty cap is modest, the licensure process could chill capital that some struggling facilities depend on, and much depends on executive discretion. On balance the design is more disclosure-and-approval than prohibition, which limits the risk of the most dire predictions but also limits how much would change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Health Over Wealth Act in the Senate on July 25, 2024, with eight cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and that is the last action recorded for it.
The Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds, health care REITs, and for-profit health care owners are better off, because none of the licensing, escrow, disclosure, or closure-notice requirements ever took effect. Communities near at-risk facilities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and for-profit health care owners

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Over Wealth Act in the Senate on July 25, 2024.

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, Welch, Merkley, Warren, Sanders, Booker, Smith, and Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all eight were Democrats or Independents.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on the day it was introduced and never brought it to a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican cosponsored the bill; the Finance Committee, chaired by a Democrat with a Democratic Senate majority, took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would require an HHS license before buying or investing in health care entities, allow a moratorium on acquisitions while a task force studies abuses, mandate escrow accounts, force public disclosure of fees, dividends, and political spending, and require divestment on license revocation. Private equity's returns in health care come largely from deals and fees the bill would expose and, in some cases, block.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill bans sale-leaseback deals that would weaken a hospital's long-term finances and removes rent from health care properties from income that qualifies a company for REIT tax status, eliminating a tax benefit on sale-leaseback arrangements whose costs fall on the hospitals and the communities they serve.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital, nursing home, and physician-practice owners
industries.note: All for-profit health care owners would face reporting on debt, staffing, wage cuts, closures, executive pay, and political spending, with civil penalties for violations and hospital closure rules on top. The compliance costs serve transparency the public currently does not have.

industries.industry: Registered investment companies and asset managers
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for registered investment companies to strip assets from health care entities or undermine care quality and access, a narrow rule that mainly constrains aggressive deal structures while ordinary index-style investment continues.
